column.title: The air needs no lid: gravity holds it
column.mini: Molecules thrown about at the speeds of a gas, pulled down by gravity, with no ceiling: their numbers fall off exponentially with height, as the barometric formula says and as balloons measure.
column.text: Seven hundred molecules move with the random speeds of a gas at a fixed temperature, are pulled down by gravity and bounce off the ground. There is no ceiling; the ones that fly out of the frame fall back. Counted slice by slice, they follow the exponential law of the barometric formula, p = p₀ e^(−h/H), with H = kT/(mg), 8.4 km for air at 15 °C [2]. The real atmosphere does the same: half the sea-level pressure at 5.5 km, a hundredth at 31 km, a millionth near 100 km, with no edge [1]. A gas next to a vacuum would spread out without gravity; with it, it forms a column that never meets a wall.
column.verdict: Would favour a container: a pressure that stays nearly constant with height and drops to zero at a definite altitude.
radio.title: Which radio waves the ionosphere sends back
radio.mini: Short waves bounce off the electron layers 100–300 km up and reach beyond the horizon in hops; higher frequencies go straight through to the satellites. On a round Earth one hop is at most about 3,800 km.
radio.text: Above 60 km, sunlight frees electrons from the air and builds the D, E and F layers. A radio wave is turned back where its frequency equals the local plasma frequency, f_p = 8.98 √N_e, and an oblique wave up to f_oF2 / cos φ [1]. Long waves follow the ground and, by day, are absorbed; short waves (3–30 MHz) bounce beyond the horizon in hops, with a silent skip zone near the transmitter; VHF, UHF and microwaves go through, which is why FM radio reaches only the horizon and satellites use high frequencies. The longest single hop leaves and returns grazing the ground: on a sphere 2R arccos(R/(R+h)), 3,836 km for a layer at 300 km, matching the hops of up to about 4,000 km that HF predictions use [2]. The section of the Earth is drawn at true scale.
radio.verdict: Would favour the flat model: VHF and microwave links routinely working far beyond the line of sight with no satellite or relay, or single short-wave hops far longer than 4,000 km.
heat.title: Why satellites do not melt in a thousand-degree thermosphere
heat.mini: At 400 km the thin air is at about 1,000 K, but it has 240 billion times fewer molecules than at sea level: its impacts bring under a milliwatt per square metre, against 1,361 W/m² of sunlight.
heat.text: Temperature measures how fast molecules move; heat is how much energy reaches a body each second, and that depends on how many molecules strike it. At 400 km, where the ISS flies, the gas is at about 1,000 K, but with 10¹⁴ molecules per cubic metre [1]. Striking a surface at room temperature, they bring (n v̄/4) · 2k(T_gas − T_wall), about 0.6 mW per square metre [2]; the same gas at sea-level density would bring about 100 MW/m². The satellite's own speed adds ½ρv³ ≈ 0.6 W/m² on its front. Sunlight brings 1,361 W/m² [3], and a black ball in sunlight settles at about 278 K, where what it absorbs equals what it radiates. The animation watches the same micrometre cube for the same 100 microseconds: full at sea-level density (25 million molecules, 5 × 10¹¹ impacts), nearly empty at 400 km (three impacts).
heat.verdict: Would favour the objection: a thermosphere dense enough to bring watts per square centimetre, which would also bring every satellite down within days.
rad.title: From sunlight to temperature: a plate on its orbit
rad.mini: Sunlight brings energy, the energy piles up, the temperature rises until radiation σT⁴ carries off as much as comes in. A black plate at 400 km swings between about 177 K in the Earth's shadow and 331 K in sunlight.
rad.text: A black aluminium plate of 1 m² and 2 mm (5.4 kg, heat capacity C = 4,844 J/K [4]) on an orbit at 400 km. In sunlight it absorbs P_in = αSA = 1,361 W [3]; it radiates P_out = 2εσAT⁴ from its two faces [5]. The difference is stored: C dT/dt = P_in − P_out. Cold, it warms by about 17 K a minute; the warmer it is, the more it radiates, and the rise stops at T_eq = (αS/2εσ)^(1/4) = 331 K. An orbit lasts 92.4 minutes [6], up to 36 of them in the Earth's shadow, where nothing comes in and the plate cools to about 177 K. The animation integrates the equation step by step, one orbit in 24 seconds; the Earth's own reflected light and infrared are left out. The thermosphere's gas adds less than a milliwatt [1][2].
rad.verdict: Would favour the objection: a satellite whose temperature followed the thermosphere's 1,000 K rather than sunlight and shadow.
krak-lap.title: One lap of the Earth, timed at every barograph of 1883
krak-lap.mini: Krakatoa's pressure wave passed the same barographs up to seven times in 1883. Between two passages of the same wave, one lap: about 36 hours one way round and 35 the other, at every station from Calcutta to Washington.
krak-lap.text: On 27 August 1883 Krakatoa's explosion sent a pressure wave round the Earth, and the Royal Society printed its passage times at some fifty barographs [1]. At one station, passage III is passage I one lap later, and IV is II one lap later in the other direction. The difference of two readings of one clock needs neither the station's position nor the time of the explosion. The laps take about 36.2 hours towards the antipodes and 34.7 hours coming back, the gap being the wind, wherever the barograph stood. On a globe one lap is 2πR/v. With the Lamb wave's 310 m/s [2], the 29 stations with a clean lap each way give R = 6,310 ± 137 km. Almost all of the uncertainty comes from the other reductions and from the speed of the wave, sized by the 2022 eruption's laps, 1.1% shorter.
krak-lap.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: laps that change with the station's position, as echoes off an edge or a dome would make them, or no regular passages after the first two.
krak-gap.title: Krakatoa 1883: the first interval against the flat model
krak-gap.mini: The hours between the first two passages of Krakatoa's wave fall on a straight line with the angle from the volcano, as a globe predicts with nothing fitted. The flat model's best echoes scatter by 3 to 7 hours.
krak-gap.text: At each 1883 barograph [1], the interval from the first passage to the second is the time to go on to the antipodes and come back: on a globe (2π − 2θ)R/v, a straight line, 28 hours near Krakatoa and 7 hours near its antipodes. The 40 stations with both times unqueried follow it with a scatter of 50 minutes, nothing fitted (R = 6,371 km, v = 310 m/s [2]). A plane has no way round, so the second passage must be an echo. Off a rim at any radius from the map's edge to 100,000 km, the best line scatters by 5.6 to 7.4 hours. Off a dome at its best height, 5,012 km, it scatters by 3.3 hours and needs a wave at 62 m/s, a fifth of the speed of sound.
krak-gap.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the intervals following the distances of an echo on the flat map rather than the angle from the volcano on the globe.
tonga.title: Hunga Tonga 2022: the Earth's radius from barometers
tonga.mini: The pressure wave of the Hunga Tonga eruption passed 102 US weather stations twice, once each way round the planet. From the two times alone, at the speed the air's temperature fixes: R = {{tgR}} ± {{tgS}}. A flat plane has no path for the second passage.
tonga.text: On 15 January 2022 the Hunga Tonga volcano exploded and sent a pressure pulse, a Lamb wave, round the whole atmosphere [2]. Every US airport weather station logs its barometer once a minute, and the logs are open [1]. At each of 102 stations the pulse arrives once the short way round, after t₁ = Rθ/v, and again the long way, after t₂ = R(2π − θ)/v, where θ is the angle from the volcano and v about 310 m/s, the speed computed from the air's temperature [3]. Their sum gives one lap, 2πR/v, whatever the station's place. The {{tgN}} stations that saw both passages clearly give R = {{tgR}} ± {{tgS}} (95 %: {{tgLo}}–{{tgHi}} km), with nothing fitted; the mean radius is 6,371 km. A flat plane, given its own speed and start time, fits the first passage with a scatter of 27 minutes against the globe's 8, and needs the wave to go at 427 m/s; for the second passage it has no path at all, and its best echo off a rim scatters by 80 minutes or more.
tonga.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: each barometer recording the pulse only once, or a second passage whose time follows an echo off an edge rather than the long way round a ball.
krakatoa.title: Krakatoa 1883: one lap of the Earth at every barograph
krakatoa.mini: In 1883 Krakatoa's pressure wave passed some fifty barographs up to seven times. Between two passages in the same direction, one lap: about 36 hours one way round and 35 the other, at every station. With the speed of 2022's wave: R = {{krR}} ± {{krS}}.
krakatoa.text: On 27 August 1883 Krakatoa's explosion sent a pressure wave round the Earth, and the Royal Society printed its passage times at some fifty barographs, read by hand [1]. At one station, passage III is passage I one lap later, and IV is II one lap later the other way round: the difference of two readings at the same place is one lap, 2πR/v, with no position and no eruption time needed. With the Lamb-wave speed of about 310 m/s [2], the {{krN}} stations with a clean lap in each direction give R = {{krR}} ± {{krS}} (95 %: {{krLo}}–{{krHi}} km); the mean radius is 6,371 km. The same laps, about 36 hours one way round and 35 the other, are found from Calcutta to Washington. A flat map's echoes off a rim or a dome would make the lap change with the station's place; their best fits to the first interval scatter by 3 to 7 hours.
krakatoa.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: laps that change with the station's position, as echoes off an edge or a dome would make them, or no regular passages after the first two.
